meta.blurb: By three o'clock every afternoon, Hana's energy has vanished. Her colleague Dev, a running coach, helps her test what really gives steady energy: sleep, light, meals, movement and stress, with the evidence for each.
meta.bible: Hana: an office worker of about thirty-five whose energy drops every afternoon; practical, tired and funny. Dev: her colleague, a part-time running Coach who reads about health; calm, encouraging and careful to say what is proven and what is not. The story runs over about four weeks in a busy office, a park and Hana's flat. Key terms: Energy, Calories, Cells, Body clock, Circadian rhythm, Daylight, Adenosine, Caffeine, Blood sugar, Glucose, Insulin, Fibre, Protein, Whole grains, Glycaemic index, Dehydration, Iron, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Diabetes, Glucose monitor, Adrenal fatigue, Registered dietitian. Facts: the body turns food and oxygen into usable energy inside every cell; the afternoon dip in alertness is partly driven by the body clock and happens even without lunch; adults are usually advised to sleep at least seven hours; caffeine blocks the brain's sleepiness signal, can stay in the body for many hours, and for most adults up to about four cups of coffee a day is considered safe, and less in pregnancy; blood sugar rises after meals in every healthy person and the body brings it back down with insulin; fibre, protein and fat slow digestion; several small trials found that a short walk after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar; regular exercise reduces tiredness in trials; adrenal fatigue is not a recognised medical condition; alcohol can help people fall asleep but harms the quality of sleep. Foods: Oats, Beans, Lentils, Eggs, Yoghurt, Nuts, Fruit, Vegetables, Wholemeal bread, Brown rice, Coffee, Tea, Water. Safety facts: tiredness that lasts for weeks, or comes with extreme thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, low mood or breathlessness, needs a doctor and not a diet; people with diabetes, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should follow their doctor's advice and ask a doctor or registered dietitian before changing their diet; do not take iron pills unless a doctor advises it. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

beats.summary: Her colleague Dev, a running coach who reads about health, offers to help her test what works.

beats.summary: Every cell turns food and oxygen into usable energy; calories measure the energy in food.

beats.summary: The body has a clock of about twenty-four hours, and the afternoon dip in alertness is partly caused by it.

beats.summary: Morning daylight helps to set the body clock; going outside early may help alertness and sleep.

beats.scene: A dark bedroom with a clock showing eleven and a lamp switched off
beats.summary: Adults are usually advised to sleep at least seven hours a night, and sleep is the base of daytime energy.

beats.scene: A plate of biscuits and crisps beside a yawning person at a night desk
beats.summary: After short sleep people tend to feel hungrier and crave sweet food, so poor sleep can look like a food problem.

beats.summary: Caffeine blocks the brain's sleepiness signal; it can stay in the body for many hours, so late coffee can harm sleep.

beats.summary: Hana moves her coffee to the morning and stops drinking it after lunch to protect her sleep.

beats.summary: Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose, the sugar in the blood; the body uses insulin to move it into cells.

beats.summary: Blood sugar rises after every meal in every healthy person and then falls; this rise and fall is normal.

beats.summary: Foods that are digested quickly, such as sugary drinks and white bread, raise blood sugar faster than foods rich in fibre.

beats.summary: Fibre, protein and fat slow down digestion, so a balanced meal raises blood sugar more gently.

beats.summary: Whole grains and beans digest slowly and keep their fibre, so they are better for steady energy than refined grains.

beats.scene: A plate where vegetables sit first on the fork and bread waits beside it

beats.scene: Hana and Dev walk around a park in coats after eating lunch
beats.summary: A short walk after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar in several small trials and may reduce sleepiness.

beats.scene: A tall fizzy drink with sugar cubes stacked beside it in a cinema
beats.summary: Sugary drinks raise blood sugar quickly without making you feel full; water, tea and coffee without sugar are better.

beats.scene: Hana fills a water bottle at an office tap beside a colour chart
beats.summary: Even mild dehydration can lower focus and mood; thirst guides most healthy people, and drinks and food both supply water.

beats.scene: Hana opens a desk drawer holding a banana, nuts, yoghurt and an apple

beats.scene: A big bowl of warm food beside a thin salad on a table

B1B2: Every afternoon at three o'clock, Hana's energy disappears and her eyes begin to close. She reaches for a strong coffee and a sweet biscuit, although she knows that they will not help for long.
Her colleague Dev coaches a running club in the evenings, and he reads a lot about health. He offers to help Hana test what really gives steady energy, and what is only a story.
Dev explains that every cell in the body turns food and oxygen into usable energy. Calories are a way of measuring how much energy there is in food.
The body has an inner clock that runs for about twenty-four hours, and it makes us more alert at some times and sleepier at others. The afternoon dip is partly caused by this clock.
Daylight is the main signal that sets the body clock. Going outside in the morning, even for a short walk, may help alertness during the day and sleep at night.
Adults are usually advised to sleep at least seven hours a night. Sleep is the base of daytime energy, and nothing else works well without it.
After short nights, people often feel hungrier and crave sweet, fatty food. Small trials suggest that sleeping less changes hunger signals in the body.
Caffeine blocks a signal that tells the brain it is tired, but it does not remove the tiredness. It can stay in the body for many hours, so a late coffee can harm sleep.
Hana decides to drink her coffee in the morning and to stop after lunch. The first afternoons are hard, but her sleep slowly improves.
When we eat carbohydrates, the body breaks them down into glucose, the sugar in the blood. A hormone called insulin helps to move the glucose into the cells.
Blood sugar rises after every meal, even in healthy people, and then falls again as insulin does its work. This rise and fall is normal, and it is not a sign of illness.
Foods that are digested quickly, such as sugary drinks and white bread, raise blood sugar fast. Foods that are rich in fibre, such as beans and oats, raise it more slowly.
Fibre, protein and healthy fat slow down digestion, so a balanced meal raises blood sugar more gently. A plate of bread alone is a faster, bigger rise.
Whole grains, such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread, keep their fibre and digest more slowly. Beans and lentils do this too, and they also contain protein.
Some people feel sleepy after a big sweet meal, and a blood sugar swing is one possible reason. The evidence is mixed, and the afternoon dip also happens without any meal.
There is no single best breakfast that suits everyone in the world. A breakfast with fibre and protein, such as porridge with nuts or eggs on wholemeal toast, suits many people.
Some small studies suggest that eating vegetables and protein before bread or rice lowers the rise in blood sugar. The evidence is early, but it costs nothing to try.
Several small trials show that a ten to fifteen minute walk after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar. It is also a pleasant way to wake up.
Sugary drinks give a fast rise in blood sugar and no feeling of fullness. Water, tea and coffee without sugar are better everyday drinks.
Even mild dehydration can lower focus and mood in some people. For most healthy people, thirst and pale yellow urine are a good guide to when to drink.
A snack with fibre and protein, such as an apple with nuts or a yoghurt with fruit, keeps energy steadier than sweets. Hana fills a drawer at her desk with snacks like these.
Eating too little food can cause tiredness, because the body needs enough energy. Very strict diets can drain energy, and anyone who is very active needs more food.
Dev sketches a steady plate: about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, and a quarter protein. It is not a rule, but it is a good starting point.
On Sunday, Hana cooks a big pot of beans and vegetables and fills several boxes. Having meals ready makes it much easier to eat well on busy days.
Hana starts to bring a lunch of lentil salad, vegetables, wholemeal bread and fruit. It costs little and keeps her energy steadier through the afternoon.
A big meal very late at night may disturb sleep for some people. Finishing dinner a few hours before bed, when possible, is a sensible idea.

Iron helps the blood to carry oxygen, and a lack of it can cause tiredness. Beans, lentils, leafy greens, meat and fortified cereals contain iron, and vitamin C helps the body to absorb the iron from plants.
Vitamin pills do not give extra energy to most people. They help only if the body is short of a vitamin, and a doctor can check this with a simple test.
Energy drinks contain caffeine and often a lot of sugar. They give a short boost followed by a drop, and they are not advised for children.
It seems backwards, but regular exercise reduces tiredness in trials. Even a short walk can raise alertness for a while, so moving can be a way to get energy.
Sitting for many hours is linked with poorer health. Standing up and moving for a minute or two every half hour breaks up long sitting.
Muscles use sugar from the blood, so building muscle helps the body to use energy well. Guides advise strengthening exercise at least twice a week.
Stress hormones raise blood sugar and can leave a person tired. Slow breathing and short breaks may help a little, and talking to someone helps too.
Long periods of concentration use up mental energy over time. Short breaks help attention, and no brain works well for hours without a rest.
Alcohol can help people to fall asleep, but it makes sleep lighter and more broken later in the night. A drink in the evening can mean a tired morning.
Bright light at night can delay the body clock. Dimmer lights and less screen time before bed may help you to fall asleep.
A cool, dark and quiet bedroom helps most people to sleep. Waking up at about the same time every day also helps the body clock.
A short nap of about twenty minutes can improve alertness. A longer nap may leave you groggy, and napping late in the day can harm sleep at night.
Many people crave something sweet in the afternoon, and this is very common. Poor sleep, stress, or a long time without eating can all increase cravings, and planning helps.
Adrenal fatigue is not a recognised medical condition, and products that promise to fix it have no good evidence. Real tiredness does have real causes, and a doctor can look for them.
Wearable glucose monitors are very useful for people with diabetes. For healthy people the benefit is unclear, and the readings can cause needless worry.
Tiredness that lasts for weeks, or comes with other signs, needs a doctor and not a new diet. Examples are low mood, breathlessness, or losing weight without trying.

Very strong thirst, passing urine very often, blurred vision, weight loss that cannot be explained, and tiredness may be signs of diabetes. Anyone with these signs should see a doctor as soon as possible.
Hana keeps an energy diary for two weeks, writing down her sleep, meals, movement and mood. A diary helps to find patterns that are easy to miss.
Hana reads her diary for the last two weeks and sees a pattern. Her best days follow a good night and a walk, and her worst follow a short night and a skipped lunch.
Time with friends, and doing things that matter to us, support energy and mood too. These things are harder to measure, but they are a real part of a good day.
After four weeks, Hana's afternoons are much better, although not perfect. Dev reminds her that one person's result is not proof, and that some days are still hard.
Dev says that energy is like a bank account. Sleep, food, movement and rest are deposits, and no single one can cover everything.
Some people have long-term conditions that cause tiredness, and for them a few lifestyle tips are not enough. They deserve kindness and a doctor's help, not blame or quick fixes.
This book is general information and is not medical advice. If you have a health condition, a pregnancy or a child to feed, ask a doctor or a registered dietitian first.
C1C2: Every afternoon at three o'clock, the energy drains out of Hana like water from a bath, and the numbers on her screen begin to swim. She reaches for a strong coffee and a sweet biscuit, as she has done for years, although she suspects that this habit is part of the problem and not the answer. Today she decides to find out what a person can really do about it.

Hana's colleague Dev spends his evenings coaching a running club, and he spends his lunch breaks reading about sleep, food and exercise. He offers to help her test what really gives steady energy and what is only a popular story, and he promises to tell her plainly whenever the evidence is weak. Hana, who has tried three miracle teas, says that she would be grateful for some honesty.

Dev explains that every cell in the body turns the food that we eat and the oxygen that we breathe into energy that it can use. Calories are simply a way of measuring how much energy a food contains, and they say nothing about how a person will feel a few hours after eating it. Hana writes in her notebook that energy is a matter of fuel, air and timing.

Dev tells Hana that the body has an inner clock, called the circadian rhythm, that runs for about twenty-four hours and makes people more alert at some times of day and sleepier at others. Most people feel a dip in the early afternoon, even if they have eaten nothing at all, so the slump that Hana feels is partly the work of her clock. It is quite normal, Dev says, and it is certainly not a personal failing or a sign that something is wrong.

Light is the strongest signal that sets the body clock, and morning daylight in particular tells the brain that the day has begun. Going outside early, even on a grey day, may help people to feel more alert and to sleep better at night, although the research is still growing and the effect differs from person to person. Hana decides to drink her first coffee in the park instead of at her desk.

Most guides advise adults to sleep at least seven hours a night, and some people need a little more. Sleep is the base of daytime energy, and Dev says that no food, drink or exercise can fully make up for a week of short nights. Hana admits, with some embarrassment, that she usually sleeps for five and a half hours and then wonders why she is tired.

After short nights, many people feel hungrier and crave sweet, fatty foods, and small trials have shown that sleeping less changes the hormones that control hunger. This means that a craving for biscuits at three o'clock may be a sleep problem dressed up as a food problem, and Hana laughs when she realises that her biscuit habit might start in bed. She resolves to treat her bedtime as seriously as her breakfast, and to protect it from late television.

Caffeine works by blocking adenosine, a chemical that builds up during the day and tells the brain that it is time to rest, but it does not remove the tiredness. It can stay in the body for many hours, so a coffee drunk at four in the afternoon can still be at work at bedtime and can make sleep lighter. Dev adds that for most adults up to about four cups of coffee a day is considered safe, and less is advised in pregnancy.

Hana decides to drink her coffee in the morning and to stop after lunch, so that the caffeine has time to leave her body before bedtime. The first few afternoons are hard, and she feels a headache and a heavy fog, but within a week she is falling asleep faster and waking up less often. Dev says that this is a small experiment with a promising result, though only one person has tested it.

When we eat carbohydrates such as bread, rice, fruit and potatoes, the body breaks them down into glucose, which is the sugar that circulates in the blood. A hormone called insulin helps to move the glucose into the cells, where it can be used for energy or stored, and in a healthy body this system keeps blood sugar within a fairly narrow range. Hana says that she had always imagined sugar as something that comes only from sweets.

Blood sugar rises after every meal in every healthy person, and then falls again as insulin moves the glucose into the cells, so a rise is a normal part of eating and not a sign of illness. How large the rise is depends on what is eaten, how fast it is digested and the person who eats it, and even the same person can react differently on different days. Dev says that the goal is a gentler wave and not a flat line.

Foods that are digested quickly, such as sugary drinks, sweets and white bread, send glucose into the blood fast, while foods rich in fibre, such as oats, beans and lentils, release it more slowly. A scale called the glycaemic index ranks foods in this way, but Dev says that it is only a rough guide, because what people eat together and how it is cooked also change the result. Hana looks at her usual lunch of white bread and a fizzy drink and winces.

Fibre, protein and healthy fat all slow digestion, which means that a balanced meal raises blood sugar more gently than a plate of plain starch or sugar. Adding beans to rice, nuts to fruit or an egg to toast is an easy way to turn a fast meal into a slower one, and it costs very little extra effort. Dev says that this is one of the best-supported ideas in the field, although it will not make anyone feel perfect.

Whole grains such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread keep their outer layers, so they contain more fibre and are digested more slowly than refined grains such as white bread. Beans and lentils do the same, and they add protein and minerals as well, which makes them some of the best foods for a long, steady release of energy. Hana swaps her white sandwich for wholemeal bread with hummus and finds, to her surprise, that she prefers it.

Many people talk about a spike and a crash, and some do feel sleepy after a big, sweet meal, so a swing in blood sugar may be one reason. The evidence is mixed, however, and Dev reminds Hana that the afternoon dip also happens in people who have eaten nothing, so food is only part of the explanation. Good advice, he says, should never promise more than the science can honestly deliver to the person who is listening.

Dev says that there is no single best breakfast, and that some people feel perfectly well without eating one at all. A breakfast that contains fibre and protein, such as porridge with nuts and seeds or eggs on wholemeal toast, seems to suit many people because it keeps them full until lunch. Hana, who used to eat a pastry on the way to work, makes porridge the night before and feels more alert by ten.

Some small studies suggest that eating vegetables and protein at the start of a meal, and bread or rice towards the end, lowers the rise in blood sugar afterwards. The evidence is still early and the studies were small, but the trick costs nothing, and Dev says that it does not harm anybody to start a meal with a salad. Hana tries it at lunch and notices only that her salad tastes better when she is hungry.

Several small trials show that a gentle walk of ten to fifteen minutes after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar, because working muscles take up glucose from the blood. It is also a pleasant way to wake up the brain, and Dev says that it is the cheapest advice in the whole book. Hana begins to take a short lap of the park every day after lunch, and the three o'clock slump becomes a little less heavy.

Sugary drinks deliver a large dose of sugar with no fibre, so the blood sugar rises quickly and the person does not feel full, which makes it easy to drink more. Water, tea and coffee without sugar are better everyday choices, and the World Health Organization advises that free sugars should provide less than ten percent of daily energy. Hana measures the sugar in her favourite fizzy drink and decides that it is a dessert and not a drink.

Even mild dehydration can make some people feel tired, less focused and a little irritable, and Hana, who drinks mostly coffee at work, is not surprised. For most healthy people, thirst and pale yellow urine are a good guide to when to drink, and foods such as soup, fruit and vegetables supply water too. Dev suggests that she keeps a bottle on her desk, and she soon discovers that she finishes it without thinking.

Hana stocks her desk drawer with snacks that combine fibre and protein, such as an apple with peanut butter, a handful of nuts, plain yoghurt with berries or a boiled egg. These keep energy steadier than sweets because they are digested more slowly, and they make the three o'clock cravings much easier to resist. Dev notes that he also eats the occasional biscuit, because no food needs to be a villain.

Eating too little food can cause tiredness, poor concentration and bad moods, because the body needs enough energy to do its work. Very strict diets can drain energy, and people who are very active, growing or pregnant need more food than they might expect, so Dev says that the aim is steady energy and not the smallest possible plate. Hana, who skips breakfast and lunch when she is busy, confesses that she has been running on empty.

Dev sketches a steady plate on the back of an envelope, with about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains or other starchy foods, and a quarter protein, plus a little healthy oil. It is not a strict rule, he says, and it will look different in different countries and on different budgets, but it is a good starting point for most healthy adults. Hana sticks the envelope to the side of her computer, where she can see it every time she plans her lunch.

On Sunday afternoon, Hana cooks a large pot of beans and vegetables with a pan of brown rice and fills several boxes for the week ahead. Having meals ready makes it much easier to eat well on busy days, because the choice has already been made, and Dev says that planning is the secret ingredient that no advertisement ever sells. By Wednesday her boxes are empty, her purse is a little fuller, and she feels rather pleased with her own organisation.

Hana starts to bring her own lunch, usually a lentil and vegetable salad with olive oil, a slice of wholemeal bread and a piece of fruit. It costs less than the shop sandwich, it is rich in fibre and protein, and it keeps her energy noticeably steadier throughout the afternoon. Dev says that it is only one person's experience, and not proof, but he admits that the results make him smile.

A big meal late at night may disturb sleep in some people, and lying down soon after eating can make heartburn more likely. Finishing dinner a few hours before bed, when this is possible, is a sensible idea, although people who work at night or who have different routines will need to find what works for them. Hana, who often eats a large dinner at ten, tries moving it earlier and is surprised by how much better she sleeps.

Iron helps the blood to carry oxygen around the body, and a lack of iron is one common cause of tiredness, particularly in women who have heavy periods. Beans, lentils, leafy greens, meat and fortified cereals contain iron, and vitamin C from fruit or vegetables helps the body to absorb the iron from plants, but iron pills should never be taken unless a doctor advises them. Hana adds a squeeze of lemon to her lentils and makes a note to ask her doctor about a blood test.

Advertisements often suggest that vitamin pills give extra energy, but they do so only if the body is short of the vitamin in question, such as vitamin B12 or vitamin D. A doctor can check for a lack with a simple blood test, which is far more reliable than guessing. Most healthy people who eat a varied diet do not need a supplement at all, although some groups, such as pregnant women, may be advised to take one, so Hana cancels her monthly vitamin subscription.

Energy drinks usually contain a large amount of caffeine, and many also contain a lot of sugar, so they give a short boost that is often followed by a drop. The word energy on the can only means calories, and health organisations do not advise energy drinks for children, who are more sensitive to caffeine than adults. Dev says that if Hana wants a boost, a glass of water and a walk are safer and cheaper.

It seems backwards, but regular exercise reduces tiredness in many trials, even in people who feel exhausted when they begin. Even a ten-minute walk can raise alertness for a while, so moving the body is often a better remedy for a sleepy afternoon than sitting still with another coffee. Dev says that he sees this all the time with people in his running club.

Sitting for many hours at a time is linked with poorer health and with feeling sluggish, and the effect seems to be greater when a person does little exercise elsewhere in the day. Standing up and moving around for a minute or two every thirty to sixty minutes breaks up long periods of sitting, and Hana sets a quiet reminder on her phone. By the end of the week, she has found three excellent reasons to visit the printer.

Muscles take up glucose from the blood, so keeping them strong helps the body to handle sugar and to use energy well. Many health guides advise strengthening exercises, such as lifting weights, using resistance bands or doing push-ups, on at least two days a week, in addition to activities that raise the heartbeat. Hana begins with two short sessions at home with a bottle of water in each hand.

When a person is under stress, the body releases hormones that raise blood sugar and prepare for action, and if the stress lasts for weeks it can leave a person drained. Slow breathing, short breaks, time outdoors and talking to someone can all help a little, and Dev says that someone who feels overwhelmed for a long time should see a doctor. Hana finds that three slow breaths before a difficult meeting make her calmer and a good deal clearer in her thinking.

Long periods of concentration use up mental energy, and attention gradually becomes weaker unless the brain gets a short rest. Short breaks, even for a minute or two, help attention, and the best breaks are those in which a person looks away from the screen, moves a little or has a chat with a colleague. Hana learns that a five-minute walk can do more for a difficult report than another cup of coffee.

Alcohol can help people to fall asleep faster, but it makes sleep lighter and more broken later in the night, so that a person wakes feeling less rested than usual. A drink in the evening may therefore lead to a tired morning, and Dev adds that alcohol also raises the risk of several cancers, so less is better for health in general. Hana, who often has wine on weekdays, decides to keep it for the weekend.

Bright light in the evening can delay the body clock and make it harder to fall asleep, and the effect may be greater for bright screens that are held close to the face. Dimmer lamps and less screen time in the hour before bed may help, though the strength of the effect varies, and the content on the screen matters as well. Hana puts her phone to charge in the hall instead of next to her bed.

Most people sleep best in a bedroom that is cool, dark and quiet, and waking up at about the same time every day helps the body clock to settle into a rhythm. A regular routine, such as reading for a few minutes before turning off the light, tells the body that it is time to sleep, and Dev says that consistency is worth more than perfection. Hana buys a pair of thick curtains and a cheap alarm clock, and she begins to look forward to bedtime.

A short nap of about twenty minutes in the early afternoon can improve alertness for several hours, though it will not make up for a long period of poor sleep. A longer nap may leave a person groggy, and napping late in the day can make it harder to sleep at night, so Dev suggests setting an alarm. Hana tries one on her lunch break and wakes up refreshed and slightly confused.

Cravings for something sweet in the afternoon are very common, and they are often made stronger by poor sleep, stress or a long gap since the last meal. Planning regular meals and having a sensible snack ready makes it easier to resist, but Dev adds that nobody should feel guilty about enjoying a sweet treat now and then. Hana buys a small bar of dark chocolate and savours it at the end of her lunch.

Hana finds online shops that sell supplements to cure adrenal fatigue, but Dev explains that this is not a recognised medical condition and that the products have no good evidence behind them. Real tiredness, however, does have real causes, such as poor sleep, low iron, thyroid problems, depression or other illnesses, and these deserve a proper check by a doctor. Hana closes the shopping page, feeling relieved that she has saved her money and a little wiser about advertising.

Hana has seen friends wearing small sensors that measure blood sugar all day, and she asks Dev whether she should buy one. He explains that these monitors are very useful for people with diabetes, but for healthy people the benefit is unclear, normal readings vary a great deal, and watching them closely can cause worry without improving health. She decides to spend the money on a better pair of walking shoes, which seems to her a much more certain investment.

Dev becomes serious and tells Hana that tiredness which lasts for many weeks, or which comes with other signs such as low mood, breathlessness, pain or weight loss that cannot be explained, needs a doctor and not a new diet. Many causes of fatigue are treatable, but they have to be found first, and a book about energy should never be used in place of a medical check. Hana promises to book an appointment if she is not better in a few weeks.

Dev tells Hana that very strong thirst, passing urine very often, blurred vision, weight loss without trying and constant tiredness can be signs of diabetes, a condition in which the body cannot control blood sugar well. Anyone with these signs should see a doctor soon, and people who already have diabetes should follow their own doctor's advice about food and medicine, since the tips in a book are not written for them. Hana does not have these signs herself, but she is very glad to know what they are.

Dev suggests that Hana keeps a simple diary for two weeks, noting how well she slept, what she ate, whether she moved and how she felt at ten, three and six o'clock. A diary does not prove anything, but it helps to reveal patterns that are easy to miss, such as the days after poor sleep or the days that begin with a sugary pastry. Hana ticks a box for every walk and a small star for every good night.

Hana reads through her diary and sees a pattern that she had never noticed. Her best days follow a good night's sleep and a walk after lunch, while her worst days follow a short night, a skipped lunch and too much coffee. The pattern is much clearer on paper than it ever was in her head, and Dev says that this is how a lot of good science begins.

Dev points out that energy is not only a matter of food and sleep, because time with friends, laughter and doing things that matter to a person also seem to support mood and energy. These things are harder to measure than blood sugar or hours of sleep, but they are a real part of a good day, and he says that a runner who trains alone often gives up first. Hana invites two friends for a Sunday walk and a picnic in the park, and she returns home feeling lighter than she has for months.

After four weeks, Hana reports that her afternoons are much better, although not perfect, and that she still has the odd day when she wants to put her head on the desk. Dev reminds her that one person's result is not proof, that she changed many things at once and that some days will always be harder than others. Hana says that she would still choose a better afternoon over a perfect experiment.

Dev says that energy is a little like a bank account, in which sleep, food, movement and rest are all deposits and long hours, stress and worry are withdrawals. No single deposit can cover everything, and a person who is running at a loss for months should not expect a cup of coffee to restore the balance. Hana, who has never been good with money, says that she finally understands the metaphor.

Dev reminds Hana that some people have long-term illnesses that cause deep and lasting tiredness, and for them a few healthy habits will not be enough and should never be presented as a cure. They deserve kindness, patience and proper medical support, not blame or quick fixes, and a book about energy should be used with that in mind. Hana thinks of her aunt, who has lived with such a condition for years, and decides to visit her this weekend.

That evening, Hana and Dev sit on a bench with two cups of tea and agree that steady energy comes from many small habits, such as sleep, light, regular meals, movement and calm, and not from any single trick. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, diabetes, a pregnancy, a child to feed or a medicine to take should ask a doctor first. For everyone else, the next step is small and cheap, which is to take a ten-minute walk after your next meal.
